headline: On the graph side, every by-Congress split whose training window ends right before the evaluated Congress (S1a, S1b, S2, S3) shows no detectable drift beyond train-to-train noise (a low-power test), while S1pool's test design (train 108-116, test 118) is the one split-level failure: under the base protocol it fails sponsor overlap and has about 1.7x the cold start, and even under the streaming protocol it keeps stale cross-Congress history (58% new sponsor-cosponsor pairs vs about 39%) because it skips 117 without a refit. The larger dangers are graph-construction leaks (future edges, label-bearing committee edges, a bill's own target edges in training), which must be fixed under any split.
overview:
This section asks whether a graph model sees the same kind of graph in train and test. In particular: are the test nodes known, are degree structure and homophily (the tendency to cosponsor within one's own party) stable, are the committee and subject vocabularies stable, and does any edge carry information from after the prediction time t0? The answer separates cleanly into **split conditions**, which can favour one split over another, and **construction requirements**, which every split must meet.

**Split conditions.** Cold start is an election-driven level, not a drift. For units evaluating 116-118 with a window that ends right before the evaluated Congress, 12.7%-18.4% of test positives come from legislators unseen in train; across all evaluated Congresses 109-118 the share ranges from about 8% to 20%. Allowing the evaluated Congress's own history up to intro + t0 (the `+stream` protocol) cuts this to at most 0.7% with no edge and at most 1.5% with fewer than 5 edges. For the distribution checks (bill degree, scale-normalised legislator degree, density, mean degree, homophily), **no split shows a detectable excess of failures** over chance. That is weaker evidence than it sounds: the binomial excess test has little power (S1a/S1b need 2 failures of 4 in B3 and 3 of 12 in B8 to reject), the per-split counts pool older folds, and folds evaluating 111-115 are tested against a noise reference (108-115) that contains those same Congresses. The units that matter, those evaluating 116-118, show real near-misses:
- P10 (S1a val, 116) fails scale-free legislator degree (`leg_rel` 0.135 > 0.127), and P11 is just below it (0.123).
- P12 (S1a test / S1b val, 117) fails House same-party share (t = +2.4).
- The House drop in cosponsors per bill in 118 hits S1b's test unit (P14: density / mean degree t = -2.2 / -2.3) almost as hard as S1pool's (P15: -2.3 / -2.4*). The S1pool B8 'failure' is therefore not meaningfully different from S1b. A sliding pool centred on recent Congresses shows smaller shifts (P16: -1.6 / -1.7).

Only two movements were checked against a trend: House cosponsors per bill in 118 (trend_z -1.0) and House homophily in 117 (trend_z +1.3) are classed as consistent with a linear trend over 108-115, which, with 8 points, means "not a detectable break" rather than an established trend. Legislator degree was not trend-tested: it shows a step increase at 116 (mean 301 in 115 to 396 in 116, PSI vs previous Congress 0.217) that mostly disappears after per-Congress normalisation (`leg_rel` 0.010-0.031 for 117-118). Committee codes and the post-111 subject vocabulary leave virtually no unseen nodes (<= 0.2% of referral edges, <= 0.04% of subject links). The one split-level FAIL is **S1pool**'s test design (evaluate 118 from 108-116): 21.7% of bills have a sponsor with no train history (bound 14.4%). Under the base protocol it also has 31.5% cold positives (vs 18.1%-18.4% for adjacent 118 windows). Under streaming those node and sponsor penalties mostly vanish, but 58.3% of positives are new sponsor-cosponsor pairs (vs 38.8%-39.4%), because train-period history is one Congress stale.

**Construction requirements** (apply to every split, including random): only about 48% of a Congress's final cosponsor graph exists at intro + t0, so the graph must be time-masked for both evaluation *and* training examples. Training with a bill's own target edges in the graph costs a simple ranker 1.8 points of Recall@20 (95% CI -3.1 to -0.3). The absence of any non-referral committee edge fully determines the Task-2 negative class (0 of 92,423 advanced). 42.7% of related-bill links point to later-introduced bills. Subjects are essentially absent at t0 (about 1% of young bills), and policy area is present for only 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56).

**What is inferred, not shown.** The noise bands come from 7-8 overlapping Congresses, so the tests have modest power and only approximate independence. Degree statistics use final snapshots. The at-t0 coverage figures are proxies from the in-progress 119th Congress. The cost of inconsistent training is measured with a 3-feature linear ranker, not a GNN.

B-c43-txt.interpretation: Sets the scale of the graph checks: 6,083 member-Congress rows (1,369 distinct legislators), 1,920,006 active cosponsorships, and 294,865 Task-1 positive edges at t0 = 0 (232,856 at t0 = 7; fewer because cosponsors who joined in the first week are already known at t0 = 7 and do not count as targets). The 35 evaluation units of S1a, S1b, S2, S3 and S1pool reduce to 16 distinct (train Congresses, evaluated Congress) pools, P01-P16. Several splits reuse the same pool (for example P12, train 108-116 evaluated on 117, is S1a test, S1b val, an S3 fold and S1pool test), so per-split verdicts below are not independent pieces of evidence.
B-c43-txt.caveats: Because pools overlap, a single unusual Congress (for example 118) can drive the verdict for several splits at once.

B-c45-txt.interpretation: Every election brings in new legislators: 9.5%-19.6% of members in 109-118 had never served in any earlier Congress in the data, with peaks in 112 (19.6%, after the 2010 election) and 116 (18.2%, after 2018). For the candidate pools that evaluate 116-118, legislators unseen in train account for 12.7%-18.4% of Task-1 positive edges when the train window ends right before the evaluated Congress (P10-P14, P16). The exception is P15 (train 108-116, evaluated on 118, used only by S1pool), at 31.5%, because 117 is skipped and two elections' worth of newcomers pile up. Across all units, the per-split maxima are S1a 18.0%, S1b 18.1%, S2 20.5%, S3 20.4% (the last two from folds evaluating 112). Moving between chambers is rare (0.5%-1.4% of members).
B-c45-txt.caveats: Recorded as INFO, not a split criterion: a learned per-legislator embedding (an ID embedding) cannot score about one in six test positives under any by-Congress split, so the cure is the protocol and the model (B1b/B1c), not the choice of split. 109 is understated because 108 is the first Congress in the data (left-censoring).

B-c45-o1.interpretation: The four series track each other closely. The shares of new members, of new active cosponsors and of positive edges involving a new legislator all rise and fall with elections (lowest in 109, 8.3% of positive edges; highest in 112, 20.4%; again about 18% in 116 and 118). So newcomers cosponsor at roughly the same rate as everyone else from their first Congress on. The new-to-chamber line stays near 1% throughout. Nothing here trends upward: cold start is a recurring, election-driven level of about 8%-20% of positives across 109-118, not a drift that gets worse in the test Congresses.
B-c45-o1.caveats: Shares are computed from the final snapshot of each Congress. At prediction time a newcomer has even less history (see B1b).

B-c45-o2.interpretation: Member overlap decays steadily with distance between Congresses. Among members of Congress c, 79%-90% also served in c-1 (116: 81.3%, 117: 85.1%, 118: 83.4%), 65%-79% in c-2 (118 seen in 116: 70.2%), and 55%-66% in c-3. Only 15.3% of the 118th Congress also served in the 108th. A train window that skips a Congress therefore loses about 13 points of node coverage for 118 (83.4% to 70.2%), which is the mechanism behind the P15/S1pool results in B1, B2 and B9. A window far in the past covers mostly retired legislators.
B-c45-o2.caveats: Overlap is membership in the window, not activity. A legislator can be a member of a train Congress and still have few edges there.

B-c47-txt.interpretation: Once the model may use edges of the evaluated Congress dated on or before intro + t0 (the `+stream` protocol), cold start nearly disappears. Positives whose cosponsor has no edge at all fall from 12.7%-31.5% (no train edge) to 0.2%-0.7% (`cold_lt1`). Positives whose cosponsor has fewer than 5 edges fall to 0.6%-1.5% (`cold_lt5`). Of the positives involving a train-cold cosponsor, 92%-95.5% have a cosponsor with at least 5 in-Congress edges by t0 = 0 (91.2% at minimum in S4 units), and at least 95% do by t0 = 7. Both checks pass every unit: B1b, worst unit 0.71% < 2%; B1c, worst unit 1.45% < 2%. Sponsors are almost never fully cold (`spon_cold` at most 0.1%). S4 (within-Congress cut) behaves the same, with max `cold_lt5` 0.66%.
B-c47-txt.caveats: `new_ge5` is a share of positives (edges), not of legislators. Positives are weighted toward active newcomers, so the share of cold legislators with a usable neighbourhood is likely lower. Most positives also come from bills introduced well into a Congress, when newcomers have already been active; bills from the first weeks of a Congress will be much colder than these averages, and the analysis does not split results by bill date. The >= 5-edge bar is a heuristic tied to typical neighbour-sampling fan-outs, not a measured threshold for embedding quality.

B-c47-o1.interpretation: For each pool evaluating 116-118, the chart shows three levels of history. With no history from the evaluated Congress (base split), 13%-31% of positives are cold. With the evaluated Congress's history up to t0, under 1.5% have fewer than 5 edges and under 0.75% have none. The gap between the bars is the case for the streaming protocol: in-Congress history up to t0 removes over 90% of the cold-start problem, whatever the train window. P15's extra cold start (31.5%) vanishes under streaming (1.4% below 5 edges, the same as P10's 1.4%), and its `spon_cold` is 0.0%. So under streaming, what remains of the S1pool penalty is staleness of train-period history, mainly sponsor-cosponsor pair history (B9: 58.3% new pairs vs 38.8%-39.4% for adjacent 118 windows).

B-c49-txt.interpretation: In 116-118, when train ends right before the evaluated Congress, 9.1%-13.3% of law-capable bills (11.5%-14.8% of positive edges) have a sponsor who never sponsored a law-capable bill in the train Congresses (8.8%-13.2% have a sponsor who was not even a member in train). These shares sit inside the band an ordinary election produces (one-step-ahead shares 5.1%-12.6% over 109-115, 95% upper prediction bound 14.4%). The only failure is P15 (S1pool's 118 test with 117 skipped): 21.7% of bills and 25.0% of positives have a history-less sponsor, well above the bound. S2 (3-Congress window) is barely worse than S3 (13.3% vs 13.2%), so a short window does not measurably forget sponsors.
B-c49-txt.caveats: The bound comes from 7 reference Congresses (a t prediction interval with 6 degrees of freedom). It is coarse, but P15's 21.7% exceeds it by a wide margin, so the verdict is robust for the base protocol. Under the streaming protocol sponsors are essentially never fully cold (B1b `spon_cold` <= 0.1%, 0.0% for P15), so this FAIL matters mainly for models that lean on sponsor history from the train Congresses, not on in-Congress history.

B-c51-txt.interpretation: Bill degree (cosponsors per bill) is stable. The mean is 10.2-13.9 in every Congress, and PSI (population stability index, a binned measure of distribution shift) against train pools is 0.003-0.066, far below the fixed 0.191 noise bound. Legislator degree shows an untested step: mean cosponsorships per legislator were 240-357 in 108-115 and 372-396 in 116-118, with the jump at 116 (301 to 396, PSI vs 115 = 0.217). One pool exceeds the raw bound (P11, 113-115 to 116: 0.423 > 0.390), and P10 is at 0.353. After dividing degree by the Congress mean (`leg_rel`), P10 (S1a val, 116) still fails (0.135 > 0.127) and P11 is just below it (0.123), while 117-118 are tiny (0.010-0.031). Per split, no excess of failures is detectable (raw: S2 2 of 16, p = 0.19, all others 0; scale-free: 0-1 per split, all p >= 0.185).
B-c51-txt.caveats: The per-split verdict is weak evidence. The binomial test has little power: with 4 tests (S1a, S1b) it needs 2 failures to reject, so a single failing unit, like P10's, cannot flag a split. The per-split lines pool all folds, so older folds dilute 116-118. Folds evaluating 111-115 are compared against a noise reference (108-115) that includes those Congresses, which widens the reference and biases toward PASS. Degrees use final snapshots (a proxy for as-of-t0 graphs). A pass means "not detectably different", not "identical"; the 116 step is real and argues for per-Congress normalised degree features.

B-c51-o1.interpretation: Concentration measures move slowly. Bill-degree Gini (inequality of cosponsor counts across bills) drifts down from about 0.80 (109, 112) to 0.74 (118). The share of bills with no cosponsor falls from 28%-38% in 108-112 to 19%-20% in 115-118, and the drop is concentrated around 113. Legislator Gini rises in 115-116 (0.31-0.33, up from 0.24-0.25 in 112-114), and the top-10% share stays between 0.20 and 0.23. The recent Congresses (115-118) look alike, while 108-112 look different. So a long expanding window mixes in an older regime with more zero-cosponsor bills.
B-c51-o1.caveats: These are descriptive trends with no test attached. The zero-cosponsor share matters for Task 1, because bills with no positives contribute nothing to Recall@K and should be handled consistently in train and test.

B-c53-txt.interpretation: No referral edge to a full committee ever points to a code unseen in earlier Congresses (`new_edges_full` = 0.000 in all of 109-118). Unseen subcommittee referrals are 0%-3.8% after 109 and at most 0.9% in 116-118. Per pool, unseen referral edges are 0.05%-0.19%, and the check passes every by-Congress unit (worst 1.28% < 5%). The Jaccard overlap of committee code sets is lower for expanding pools (0.50-0.62) than for sliding pools (0.72-0.91), because old pools carry codes that no longer receive referrals. This dilutes the vocabulary but does not cause unseen nodes.
B-c53-txt.caveats: As the notebook notes, codes appear to be normalised to current names, so renames are hidden rather than absent. A committee whose jurisdiction changed under the same code would pass this check but still shift in meaning. The subcommittee share of referrals also falls in 118 (19.1% vs 22%-34% earlier), which may reflect data latency for the latest Congress.

B-c55-txt.interpretation: Two different problems show up. (a) Vocabulary break: the subject thesaurus changed at 111 (vocabulary 4,247 to 957 terms, Jaccard with 110 = 0.194). After 111 the vocabulary is stable (Jaccard 0.89-0.95, new links <= 0.7%), so unseen subject links in 116-118 pools are 0.00%-0.04% and B5a passes. (b) Coverage lag: the share of law-capable bills with at least one subject falls from 96%-98% (114-116) to 61.8% in 117 and 37.2% in 118, even in the final snapshot. At prediction time it is about 1.0% (bills aged 0-30 days in the 119th, n = 732). So subjects are a post-introduction feature, and B5b records excluding them at t0 as a requirement for every split. Policy area is a separate, weaker case: near-complete in the final snapshot (99%+), but present for only 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56).
B-c55-txt.caveats: Whether subject tags also correlate with the label (for example, being tagged faster when a bill moves) is a hypothesis this section does not test; the case for exclusion rests on availability alone. The at-t0 figures come from the in-progress 119th Congress, not from timestamps on historical tags, and assuming CRS (Congressional Research Service) tagging latency was similar in earlier Congresses is an untested inference. The policy-area estimate rests on 56 bills, so excluding policy area is a softer recommendation than excluding subjects; an alternative is to use policy area with a missing indicator, but only if its assignment date can be shown to be at or before t0. Expanding pools show low Jaccard (0.20-0.22) only because they include the pre-111 thesaurus.

B-c55-o1.interpretation: The chart shows the 111 thesaurus break as a single dip in Jaccard (to 0.19), with continuity of about 0.9 elsewhere. It also shows subject coverage collapsing from 98% (116) to 62% (117), 37% (118) and 24% (119), while policy-area coverage stays flat at about 99%. The coverage collapse coincides exactly with the test Congresses. A model given subject features would see fully tagged training bills and mostly untagged test bills, a pipeline artefact that would make every temporal split look worse and every random split look better.
B-c55-o1.caveats: Final-snapshot policy-area coverage says nothing about availability at t0. See the 14.3% at-t0 proxy in the text output.

B-c57-txt.interpretation: Related-bill links are stored almost only within a Congress. Across 108-117 there are zero links to earlier or later Congresses, and in 118 only 36 earlier and 20 later, so cross-split leakage through this relation is negligible (B6a, 0.014%). Within a Congress, however, 39%-44% of related links point to a bill introduced after the source bill (42.7% overall, B6b FAIL). 30%-38% point more than 7 days ahead and 21%-32% more than 30 days ahead. In a snapshot at intro + t0, these links connect a bill to bills that do not yet exist.
B-c57-txt.caveats: Links carry no creation timestamp. Even links whose target was introduced before t0 may have been added later, for example when CRS records identical bills, so filtering by target introduction date is necessary but may not be sufficient. The "no cross-Congress links" result reflects how the source stores the data, not proof that no such relation exists.

B-c59-txt.interpretation: Committee rows mix the referral (78%-86% of rows) with post-introduction activity: markup, hearing or discharge (10%-14%) and "reported" (3.8%-7.5%). Not having any non-referral committee edge fully determines the negative class: 0 of 92,423 such bills advanced. Having one raises the rate to 33.5% (n = 18,379), since such an edge is a necessary condition for advancement. A graph that keeps these edges hands Task 2 a near-label under any split, temporal or random. Also, 12.6%-27.1% of referral edges occur after day 7, a share that falls over time (27% in 108, about 13% in 116-118). So the t0 = 7 snapshot keeps slightly more of the referral information in recent Congresses than in old ones.
B-c59-txt.caveats: The 0.000 rate is partly by definition, since "reported" is one of the non-referral activities, but markup and hearings are also strong post-t0 signals. The falling share of late referrals is a small structural drift between old train Congresses and test Congresses that time-masking reproduces faithfully but does not remove.

B-c61-txt.interpretation: Per chamber, density (edges / (bills x members)), mean cosponsors per bill and same-party share of cosponsorships mostly stay within train-to-train noise. Of the pool-centred t statistics for pools evaluating 116-118, 2 exceed |t| = 2.36: P12 (S1a test / S1b val, 117) has House same-party share at t = +2.4, and P15 (S1pool, 118 with 117 skipped) has House mean cosponsors at t = -2.4. Several others are near-misses: P14 (S1b test, 118) has House density / mean degree at t = -2.2 / -2.3, barely different from P15's -2.3 / -2.4, so the 118 House drop affects S1b's test as much as S1pool's, and P15's 'failure' is not evidence against S1pool relative to S1b. The sliding pool for 118 (P16) shows smaller shifts (-1.6 / -1.7). No split shows an excess of failures (S1a 1/12, S1b 1/12, S2 0/48, S3 1/48, S1pool 2/18; all p >= 0.23). Against the fixed 108-115 reference, the trend check classes House cosponsors per bill in 118 (12.88, t = -2.4, trend_z = -1.0) and House homophily in 117 (0.849, t = +2.6, trend_z = +1.3) as consistent with a linear trend rather than breaks.
B-c61-txt.caveats: The binomial test needs 3 failures of 12 to reject for S1a/S1b, so it can barely flag a split; S2 and S3 counts are diluted by folds evaluating 111-115, which are partly in-sample for the 108-115 reference. The reference SD comes from 8 Congresses that share members, so the 2.36 cut-off is approximate. The six metrics per pool are positively correlated (density and mean degree within a chamber are nearly redundant). Correlated tests overdisperse the failure count, so the binomial p-values for excess are too small (anti-conservative): a PASS is not weakened by this, but correlated failures effectively count about once, not twice, which lowers power further. The trend_z check fits a line to 8 points, so 'on trend' means 'no detectable break', not an established trend.

B-c61-o1.interpretation: Party homophily rises over the period: the House goes from 72% same-party cosponsorships (108-109) to 80%-85% (116-118), and the Senate from 63%-65% to 74%-77%. The rise is mostly a step around 110-112 plus a further step in the House at 116-117, not a continuous ramp. A model trained mostly on 108-110 would over-predict cross-party cosponsors in 116-118, which favours windows that include recent Congresses or a party-match feature whose weight can be refit on the latest data.
B-c61-o1.caveats: The shares are restricted to D/R sponsor-cosponsor pairs, with independents assigned by data-derived caucus. Homophily also depends on which bills get cosponsors (composition), not only on legislator behaviour.

B-c61-o2.interpretation: Senate density is higher than House density (about 0.05 vs 0.03-0.04) and broadly flat. House density declines in the last two Congresses (0.0367 in 116, 0.0329 in 117, 0.0286 in 118, the lowest of the period). For a GNN this means fewer neighbours per House bill in the test Congress than in train. Normalised degree features or degree-robust aggregation (mean rather than sum) protect against the scale change.
B-c61-o2.caveats: Density is computed on final snapshots. 118 is complete, but late-arriving cosponsorships recorded after the snapshot could depress it slightly.

B-c63-txt.interpretation: For windows ending right before the evaluated Congress, 33%-42% of Task-1 positives in 116-118 are a (cosponsor, sponsor) pair never seen in the train Congresses. Only 11%-13% are new pairs between two legislators who were both seen; the rest involve a cold node. So pair memorisation can explain at most 58%-67% of positives depending on the Congress (57.7% for P11, 67.0% for P12), and real generalisation is needed. Skipping 117 (P15) raises the new-pair share to 58.3%, against 38.8%-39.4% for the adjacent 118 windows (about 1.5x). The check itself asks whether each split's validation Congress resembles its own test Congress. The val-test gaps (S1a 0.083, S1b 0.057, S2 max 0.144, S3 max 0.135, S1pool 0.028) all fall below the 0.168 year-to-year swing bound, so B9 passes for every split.
B-c63-txt.caveats: The bound's nested leave-one-out check gave 1 false alarm in 6, so it is not loose. S2's worst gap (0.144) is close to it. S1pool's small gap (0.028) compares val 116 with pooled test 117+118 and hides that its 118 part has a much higher new-pair share.

B-c63-o1.interpretation: The new-pair share swings between 30% and 44% from Congress to Congress (for example 29.7% in 111, 43.2% in 112, 41.3% in 116, 33.0% in 117), in step with election turnover. Sliding 3-Congress windows give a new-pair share consistently about 1 point higher than expanding windows (for example 44.0% vs 43.2% in 112, 42.3% vs 41.3% in 116), so a short window raises novelty only slightly. Any by-Congress split inherits the election-driven swing, which is a plausible contributor to val-test score gaps even under a well-built split (that link is tested in section D).

B-c65-txt.interpretation: At prediction time, only about half of a Congress's final cosponsor graph exists. For eval bills in 116-118 at t0 = 0, 52.0% of the Congress's final edges are dated after intro + t0, and about 50%-52% of the final degree of the bill's known legislator neighbours accrues later. Only 70%-75% of a bill's final 1-hop neighbourhood and 33%-40% of its 2-hop edge mass are visible at t0 = 0, rising only slightly at t0 = 7 (hop1 72%-78%, hop2 36%-43%). These shares are nearly the same in train (108-115) and eval Congresses, so masking does not create a train-test shift by itself. Skipping it, though, gives the model a mostly-future graph and, by construction, all of the bill's own Task-1 labels.
B-c65-txt.caveats: The `visible` share mostly reflects where the bill falls in the Congress's calendar (90th percentile 0.85-0.93), so it is a property of the event stream, not of individual bills. `hop1_vis` is inflated by bills with no cosponsors, which count as fully visible. Recorded as a requirement for every split, not a split criterion.

B-c65-o1.interpretation: The lines are flat across 108-118. About 46%-51% of final edges are visible at t0 = 0 (47%-52% at t0 = 7), and 48%-53% of neighbour degree accrues after t0. The temporal structure of the event stream is stationary, which supports a single time-masked snapshot procedure for every Congress. Globally, the two t0 settings see nearly the same graph (about 1 point more visible at t0 = 7). Locally they do not: the bill's own 1-hop visibility rises 3-5 points (for example 0.700 to 0.742 in 116), and Task-1 positives drop by 21% (294,865 to 232,856) because first-week cosponsors become inputs rather than targets. That bill-local difference is what matters for the ranking task.

B-c67-txt.interpretation: A 3-feature logistic ranker shows what inconsistent training inputs cost. All variants are evaluated on snapshot features. Training on final graphs that include each training bill's own target edges lowers val Recall@20 by 1.6 points (P11 to 116) and 2.0 points (P13 to 117), against 29.9%-31.0% for snapshot training. The pooled loss is 1.8 points (95% CI -3.1 to -0.3), which triggers the FAIL. The learned weights show why: the in-Congress pair count gets weight +1.54 when the target edges are present, and train positives' pair count is 3.92 in the final graph vs 1.24 in snapshots. The model learns a label-bearing feature that is much weaker at test time. Removing only the target edges from the final graph is statistically indistinguishable from snapshot training (pooled +0.7, CI -0.5 to +1.7). Dropping in-Congress features entirely costs 3.9 points (CI -5.0 to -2.8), so in-Congress history is worth keeping when it is built correctly.
B-c67-txt.caveats: This is a linear proxy with 3 count features, 3,000 training bills and 1,000 val bills per fold, on two folds. A GNN can exploit label-bearing edges more flexibly, so the true cost could be larger. P13's per-fold CI touches 0 (upper bound +0.000). The FAIL means the construction rule is binding, not that any split is invalid.

B-c67-o1.interpretation: Of the three bars per fold, only "final graph incl. own edges" is consistently negative (-0.016 and -0.020). "Final graph, own edges removed" is mixed (+0.015 and -0.001), and "no in-Congress features" is clearly negative (-0.037 and -0.041). In practice, the essential rule is to keep a training bill's own target edges out of message passing. Full snapshot replay is the safest way to guarantee that and costs nothing measurable.
B-c67-o1.caveats: Each bar is a point estimate from one fold. See the text output for the confidence intervals.

B-c69-txt.interpretation: Chamber switchers (served only in the other chamber in their latest train Congress) are 0.3%-1.0% of positives in 116-118, and party switchers are 0%-0.5%. The S3 folds show the same: 0.37%-0.99% per Congress. Switchers are ranked poorly by a sponsor-history baseline (Recall@20 3.3%-7.8%, against 22.5%-26.1% for stable legislators), but they are so few that the overall recall lost is 0.1-0.2 points per pool, below the 0.5-point tolerance, and B11 passes. By construction, all of their train edges are on other-chamber bills (`other_ch_edges` = 1.0), so their train history describes a different role.
B-c69-txt.caveats: Cold legislators have Recall@20 of exactly 0 under this baseline by construction, since they have no train counts. That says nothing about a model with in-Congress features. The party-switch recall of 65.2% for eval 111-115 rests on only 69 positives and is not meaningful. The n of 166 for 116-118 is also small.

B-c69-o1.interpretation: Stable legislators are ranked consistently across periods (sponsor_hist Recall@20 23.1% for eval 111-115 and 23.5% for 116-118), which is reassuring evidence that the baseline's mechanism does not degrade in the test Congresses. Chamber switchers are much worse (8.0% and 5.9%), and cold legislators get 0%. The party-switch bar jumps from 65% to 8%, but both bars rest on small samples (n = 69 and 166). The practical message: a chamber-specific node state, or resetting a switcher's history, would help a sliver of positives, while cold start (14,743 positives in 116-118) is the slice that actually matters.

B-c71-txt.interpretation: Section summary. Of the split conditions, 8 pass, 1 fails and 2 are INFO; 5 are construction requirements, and 2 of those need filtering (related links, B6b; training-input consistency, B12). The one split-level failure, B2 (sponsor overlap), fails only for S1pool; the worst values of B1 (31.5%) and B9's new-pair share (58.3%) also come from S1pool's 118 test, for the same reason: it evaluates 118 with a model trained on 108-116. The distribution checks (B3, B8, B9) show no detectable excess of failures for any split under the fixed 108-115 noise reference, though with low power and with unit-level near-misses on 116-118 for S1a and S1b. The requirements (B5b, B6b, B7, B10, B12) apply equally to every split, including the random split S5, so they say how to build the graph, not which split to choose.
B-c71-txt.caveats: "PASS" in a distribution check means no detectable excess over train-to-train noise, judged on 7-8 dependent reference Congresses. It is not a guarantee of equivalence.

implications: Use a by-Congress split whose training window ends immediately before the evaluated Congress, and refit on train + val before testing (S1a/S1b, or rolling S3/S2 folds). Avoid S1pool's test design (test 118 from 108-116). Under the base protocol it fails sponsor overlap (21.7% vs bound 14.4%) and has about 1.7x the cold start of adjacent 118 windows (31.5% vs 18.1%-18.4%). Under the streaming protocol those node and sponsor penalties mostly vanish (cold_lt5 1.4%, sponsor cold 0.0%), but its cross-Congress history is one Congress stale: 58.3% new sponsor-cosponsor pairs vs 38.8%-39.4% (about 1.5x), because 117 is skipped without a refit.

Adopt the streaming protocol: let the model use evaluated-Congress edges dated <= intro + t0. This removes over 90% of legislator cold start (no-edge share at most 0.7%, fewer than 5 edges at most 1.5%), and in-Congress history is worth about 3.9 Recall@20 points to a simple ranker.

Make the GNN inductive, or at least not ID-dependent: give legislator nodes features (party, chamber, tenure, in-Congress degree and pair counts as of t0) so the 12.7%-18.4% of 116-118 positives from legislators unseen in train are not scored by untrained embeddings. Reset or make chamber-specific the state of chamber switchers (<= 1% of positives, low priority).

Build every training and evaluation example from an as-of-(intro + t0) snapshot, with the target bill's own future cosponsor edges excluded from message passing. Final-graph training measurably hurts (-1.8 R@20 points pooled, 95% CI -3.1 to -0.3).

Graph schema: keep only referral committee edges dated <= t0 (lacking any other committee edge means 0 of 92,423 bills advanced), and keep related-bill links only to bills introduced <= intro + t0 (or drop the relation). Exclude legislative subjects as t0 features (about 1% available at t0; B5b requirement). Treat policy area more cautiously: it is present for 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56), so drop it unless its assignment can be timestamped at or before t0, in which case use it with a missing indicator.

Normalise degree-type features per Congress, or use mean aggregation. Legislator degree stepped up at 116 (mean 301 in 115, 372-396 in 116-118; scale-free PSI still fails for P10, 0.135 > 0.127) and House cosponsors per bill fell to 12.88 in 118 (S1b's test unit P14 at t = -2.3), so raw-count scales differ between train and test even for the recommended splits.

The graph evidence does not separate sliding (S2) from expanding (S3) windows, and small differences point both ways: S2 has 2/16 raw B3 failures vs 0/16 for S3 and a B9 max gap (0.144) closer to the 0.168 bound, but it shows smaller 118 House shifts in B8 (P16 -1.6/-1.7 vs P14 -2.2/-2.3) and no extra sponsor loss (13.3% vs 13.2%). Drift (rising homophily, the 116 degree step, the pre-113 high zero-cosponsor regime) mildly favours windows that emphasise recent Congresses, i.e. S2 or recency weighting of an expanding window. The final choice should rest on section D's backtest performance.
open_questions: Committee codes appear normalised to current names, so historical renames and jurisdiction changes are hidden. True committee schema drift is unknown.

Related-bill links have no creation timestamp, so links between bills both introduced before t0 may still have been created after t0. How much residual leakage remains after date filtering cannot be measured from this data.
The cost of inconsistent training inputs was measured with a 3-feature linear ranker on two folds. How much a GNN would exploit label-bearing or future edges, likely more, is untested.

Cold-start averages are dominated by bills introduced later in a Congress. The analysis does not show how cold the graph is for bills in the first weeks of a new Congress, when freshmen have little history even under streaming.
